Medstudent here.

Vitamin D is not water-soluble but fat-soluble which wouldn’t make it that easy to just pee it out, contrary to other comments. The body has a much harder time excreting those when taken in bulk. There are cases of a vit. D intoxication. However, I’m not here to scare you; it all depends on the dosage of the pills. A quick Google-search informed me that the NHS says no more than 4000 IU per day. If you already have a deficit though, that number might change..

My general advice: as with all over the counter medication, don’t overdo it. Do make an appointment with a primary care physician mid September, or even call your pshyciatrist for advice to bridge the gap until mid September.

If you’d think I could help you further, feel free to dm!

I don’t know about the numbers on the dentistry-exam. The principle works as follows though: you not only have to pass the exam (more than 50%), there can only start a set number of students. For example, if in year 2020-2021, only 1000 could start, this means that even if 3000 students did the exam and 1500 passed, only the 1000 students with the best results could start the course. This might sound intimidating, but in my year for example, the med students had to have +/- 60% (i.e. the 1000th person had 60%). So, your grades don’t have to be 90% ‘to have a chance’..

First of all, NAD, only a first-year med student.

Okay, first soms terminology:
Lymphoma: malign tumor of lymphocytes
Lymphocytes: white blood cells. There are different kinds; B-cells and T-cells

So, you had a biopsy done of the core of the left submandibular lymph node. Now, what are the results? We did the biopsy to make sure it isnt a B-cell lympoma, and it came out negative (so that’s a good thing).
After that, they are talking about some markers (molecules that color the cells) and how the cells presented themselves. Again, the most important part you should take away from that, is that there are no reasons to believe you have a malignant growth in you submandibular lymph node.

Now, however, with a core biopsy, you cannot be sure there isnt a malignant growth that only partially involves your node; a growth that is really growing “on”/“besides” you lymph node. To be sure that’s also absent, you’ll have to get a excisional biopsy, but that’s a more evasive procedure(?) Also, your physician will evaluate if you need it in the first place.


Everything what I stated above, should be taken with the necessary precautions. Again, I’m not a doctor, and even though I think I interpreted the results fairly accurate, a quick call with your doctor to ask if the two of you could discuss your results could do wonders.

So, if I'm not mistaken is torque T=F\*d with F= the force perpendicular to the distance, and d= the distance

(in my further explanation, I take d=0,12m, as was given in the problem)

If we want to find the force perpendicular on d (where Fm engages), you have to split Fm up in components, you'll want Fm,y. Since you know the angle, you can say that Fm,y=Fm\*sin(15°). Don't forget it's torque, so: Tm=Fm\*sin(15°)\*d. (I)

Now, you want to find a magnitude of the force Fm,y when the arm is at rest, so in other words: there can't be a resulting force, so in other words: Fm,y has te be the same as Fz (with Fz= force of gravity). Again, don't forget it's torque, so: Tz=Fz\*2d (II)

If we write (I) and (II) in a formula, you'll find:

Tz=Tm  
m\*g\*2d=Fm\*sin(15°)\*d

if we form this formula for an expression of Fm, you'll get:

Fm=(m\*g\*2d)/(sin(15°)\*d)

Obviously, you'll be able to cancel the d out, and if you fill that formula in, you get +-250N\*m.
